name: Weisswurst
description: A white sausage of minced veal and pork back fat flavoured with parsley, lemon, mace, onion and cardamom. It is the classic Munich morning sausage.
how_to_eat: Peel off the skin and eat with sweet mustard and a pretzel.
how_to_order: Order 'Weißwurst' in a Bavarian beer hall or butcher's, traditionally before noon.

name: Schweinshaxe
description: A roasted pork knuckle (ham hock) with crackling skin. It is especially popular in Bavaria, where it is called Schweinshaxn.
how_to_eat: Eat with potato dumplings or sauerkraut and a beer.
how_to_order: Ask for 'Schweinshaxe' in Bavarian beer halls and beer gardens.

name: Bavarian Pretzel
description: A lye-glazed knotted bread with coarse salt, called Brezn in Bavaria. 'Bayerische Breze' is an EU protected geographical indication since 2014.
how_to_eat: Eat plain, with butter, or alongside Weißwurst.
how_to_order: Buy a 'Brezn' at any Bavarian bakery or beer garden.

name: Obatzda
description: A Bavarian cheese spread of aged soft cheese such as Camembert mashed with butter, paprika, onion and pepper. It was granted EU PGI status in 2015.
how_to_eat: Spread on pretzels or rye bread with a beer.
how_to_order: Order 'Obatzda' as part of a Brotzeit in a beer garden.

name: Leberkäse
description: A baked loaf of finely ground pork, beef and bacon, despite its name usually containing neither liver nor cheese. It is a staple of Bavarian butcher counters.
how_to_eat: Eat a warm slice in a bread roll with mustard.
how_to_order: Ask for a 'Leberkässemmel' at a butcher's shop.

name: Nuremberg Rostbratwurst
description: Small, thin pork sausages grilled over beechwood, recorded in Nuremberg since around 1300. The name is an EU PGI and they may only be made in Nuremberg.
how_to_eat: Eat three in a roll ('Drei im Weggla') or six to twelve on a plate with sauerkraut.
how_to_order: Order 'Drei im Weggla' at a Nuremberg sausage stall.

name: Nuremberg Lebkuchen
description: Soft honey-sweetened spice cakes with nuts, a German Christmas tradition. 'Nürnberger Lebkuchen' is a protected name and must be made within the city.
how_to_eat: Eat with mulled wine at the Christmas market.
how_to_order: Buy 'Nürnberger Lebkuchen' at bakeries or the Nuremberg Christkindlesmarkt.

name: Schäufele
description: Roasted pork shoulder with crisp crackling, the signature Sunday dish of Franconia. It is served with potato dumplings and gravy.
how_to_eat: Eat with Klöße and dark beer gravy.
how_to_order: Order 'Schäufele mit Klößen' in Franconian inns.

name: Maultaschen
description: Large square pasta pockets filled with minced meat, smoked meat, spinach, bread crumbs and onion. Swabian Maultaschen are an EU PGI.
how_to_eat: Eat in broth or pan-fried with onions and egg.
how_to_order: Ask for 'Maultaschen in der Brühe' in Swabian restaurants.

name: Spätzle
description: Soft egg noodles scraped or pressed into boiling water, served as a side to meat with sauce. Swabian Spätzle have been an EU PGI since 2012.
how_to_eat: Eat as a side with roast meat and gravy.
how_to_order: Order Spätzle as a side in any Swabian inn.

name: Käsespätzle
description: Spätzle layered with grated cheese and topped with fried onions. It is traditional in Swabia, Baden and the Allgäu.
how_to_eat: Eat hot with a green salad.
how_to_order: Ask for 'Käsespätzle' in Swabian or Allgäu restaurants.

name: Black Forest Cake
description: A layer cake of cocoa sponge with cherries, Kirsch (cherry brandy) and whipped cream, decorated with chocolate shavings. It is named after the Black Forest region.
how_to_eat: Eat a slice with coffee in the afternoon.
how_to_order: Order 'Schwarzwälder Kirschtorte' at a Konditorei (cake shop).

name: Zwiebelkuchen
description: A savoury onion cake of steamed onions, diced bacon, cream and caraway on a yeast or leavened base. It is a seasonal favourite in autumn.
how_to_eat: Eat warm with new wine (Federweißer).
how_to_order: Look for 'Zwiebelkuchen' in bakeries and wine taverns in autumn.

name: Currywurst
description: A sliced pork sausage covered in curry ketchup and curry powder. It was invented in 1949 by Herta Heuwer at a stand in West Berlin.
how_to_eat: Eat with a small fork from a paper tray, usually with fries.
how_to_order: Order 'Currywurst mit Pommes' at an Imbiss stand.

name: Döner Kebab
description: Meat from a vertical rotisserie sliced into flatbread with salad and sauces. The German sandwich style developed in 1970s West Berlin from the Turkish dish.
how_to_eat: Eat wrapped in its paper, by hand.
how_to_order: Ask for 'Döner' with your choice of sauce at any kebab shop.

name: Eisbein
description: Cured and boiled pork hock. In Berlin it is traditionally served with sauerkraut and pease pudding.
how_to_eat: Eat with sauerkraut, mustard and mashed peas.
how_to_order: Order 'Eisbein mit Sauerkraut' in old Berlin pubs.

name: Berliner
description: A jam-filled yeast doughnut without a hole, fried and dusted with sugar. Berliners call it Pfannkuchen.
how_to_eat: Eat fresh, especially around New Year and Carnival.
how_to_order: Ask for a 'Pfannkuchen' at Berlin bakeries.

name: Königsberger Klopse
description: Meatballs in a creamy white sauce with capers. The dish is a classic of Berlin and eastern German home cooking.
how_to_eat: Eat with boiled potatoes and beetroot.
how_to_order: Order 'Königsberger Klopse' in traditional German restaurants.

name: Fischbrötchen
description: A bread roll filled with fish such as pickled herring, Bismarck herring or smoked mackerel, with onions, pickles and sauces. It is the typical snack of the North Sea and Baltic coasts.
how_to_eat: Eat by hand at the harbour.
how_to_order: Buy one at harbour fish stalls, e.g. Hamburg's Landungsbrücken.

name: Labskaus
description: A sailor's mash of salted or corned beef, potatoes and onion, often coloured with beetroot. It is a speciality of Bremen, Hamburg and Lübeck.
how_to_eat: Eat topped with a fried egg, pickled gherkin and rollmops herring.
how_to_order: Order 'Labskaus' in Hamburg and Bremen harbour restaurants.

name: Franzbrötchen
description: A flattened pastry roll baked with butter and cinnamon, similar to a cinnamon roll. It is Hamburg's signature bakery item.
how_to_eat: Eat with morning coffee.
how_to_order: Buy at any Hamburg bakery.

name: Rote Grütze
description: A pudding of red berries and juice thickened with starch, shared with Denmark. It is a classic Northern German dessert.
how_to_eat: Eat cold with vanilla sauce or cream.
how_to_order: Ask for 'Rote Grütze' on dessert menus in the north.

name: Grünkohl mit Pinkel
description: Stewed kale with Pinkel, a smoked groat sausage, a winter dish of northwest Germany around Bremen, Oldenburg and East Frisia. Kale outings with this meal are a winter custom.
how_to_eat: Eat with boiled or fried potatoes and mustard.
how_to_order: Order 'Grünkohl mit Pinkel' in winter in Bremen or Lower Saxony.

name: Lübeck Marzipan
description: Almond and sugar marzipan made in Lübeck to higher quality rules than ordinary marzipan. It has been an EU PGI since 1996.
how_to_eat: Eat as a sweet, often chocolate-coated.
how_to_order: Buy at Lübeck confectioners.

name: Rhenish Sauerbraten
description: A pot roast marinated for days in vinegar and spices; the Rhineland version has a sweet-sour sauce with raisins. It is regarded as a national dish of Germany.
how_to_eat: Eat with red cabbage and potato dumplings.
how_to_order: Order 'Rheinischer Sauerbraten' in Rhineland brewpubs.

name: Himmel und Erde
description: 'Heaven and earth': mashed potato with stewed apples, often served with fried blood sausage. It is popular in the Rhineland, Westphalia and Lower Saxony.
how_to_eat: Eat with sliced fried black pudding and onions.
how_to_order: Order it in Cologne brewhouses.

name: Reibekuchen
description: Fried potato pancakes, called Reibekuchen in the Rhineland and Kartoffelpuffer elsewhere. They are sold at markets and fairs.
how_to_eat: Eat hot with apple sauce or on pumpernickel.
how_to_order: Buy at Christmas markets and fairs in Cologne and Düsseldorf.

name: Kölsch
description: A clear, pale, top-fermented beer from Cologne. Since 1997 Kölsch is an EU PGI and must be brewed within about 50 km of the city.
how_to_eat: Drink from small 0.2 l 'Stange' glasses that the waiter keeps refilling.
how_to_order: Order in a Cologne brewhouse; put a beer mat on your glass when done.

name: Altbier
description: A copper-coloured, top-fermented beer brewed around Düsseldorf. Its name ('old beer') refers to the older top-fermenting method.
how_to_eat: Drink fresh in the brewery's own taproom.
how_to_order: Order 'ein Alt' in Düsseldorf's old town brewhouses.

name: Aachener Printen
description: A hard, spiced Lebkuchen from Aachen, now usually sweetened with sugar-beet syrup. The name is a protected geographical indication.
how_to_eat: Eat with coffee, especially at Christmas.
how_to_order: Buy at Aachen bakeries and confectioners.

name: Saumagen
description: A pig's stomach stuffed with pork, potatoes and carrots, then simmered and sliced. It is the signature dish of the Palatinate.
how_to_eat: Eat sliced, pan-fried, with sauerkraut and mashed potatoes.
how_to_order: Order 'Pfälzer Saumagen' in Palatinate wine taverns.

name: Frankfurt Green Sauce
description: A cold sauce of seven fresh herbs (borage, chervil, cress, parsley, burnet, sorrel, chives) with sour cream or yoghurt. The herb mix has been an EU PGI since 2016.
how_to_eat: Eat with boiled potatoes and halved hard-boiled eggs.
how_to_order: Order 'Grüne Soße' in Frankfurt apple-wine taverns in spring and summer.

name: Handkäs mit Musik
description: Handkäse, a hand-shaped sour-milk cheese, marinated in oil, vinegar and onions ('music'). It is a speciality of Frankfurt and southern Hesse.
how_to_eat: Eat with bread and butter and a glass of Apfelwein.
how_to_order: Order in Frankfurt apple-wine taverns.

name: Apfelwein
description: Tart German cider made from sour apples. In Frankfurt it is drunk from ribbed glasses and poured from a stoneware jug called a Bembel.
how_to_eat: Drink plain or mixed with sparkling water ('sauer gespritzt').
how_to_order: Order 'ein Schoppen' in a Sachsenhausen apple-wine tavern.

name: Frankfurter Kranz
description: A ring-shaped sponge cake layered with buttercream and jam and coated in caramelised nut brittle. It is the cake speciality of Frankfurt.
how_to_eat: Eat a slice with afternoon coffee.
how_to_order: Buy at Frankfurt cake shops (Konditoreien).

name: Frankfurter Würstchen
description: Thin smoked pork sausages heated in hot water, the original 'frankfurters'. They are smoked at low temperature and briefly heated in hot water before eating.
how_to_eat: Eat with mustard and bread or potato salad.
how_to_order: Order a pair at Frankfurt butchers or market stalls.

name: Thuringian Rostbratwurst
description: A long, spiced pork sausage grilled over charcoal, at least 15 cm long. The name is an EU PGI and it must be produced in Thuringia.
how_to_eat: Eat in a bread roll with mustard.
how_to_order: Buy from grill stands at Thuringian markets.

name: Thuringian Dumplings
description: Hand-shaped potato dumplings made from two-thirds raw grated and one-third cooked potato. They are Thuringia's classic side dish.
how_to_eat: Eat with roast and gravy.
how_to_order: Order 'Thüringer Klöße' with a roast in Thuringian inns.

name: Dresden Stollen
description: A Christmas fruit bread with dried fruit, nuts and spices, covered in powdered sugar. 'Dresdner Christstollen' is a protected geographical indication.
how_to_eat: Eat in slices during Advent.
how_to_order: Buy at Dresden bakeries and the Striezelmarkt.

name: Eierschecke
description: A layer cake from Saxony and Thuringia with a cake base, a quark cheesecake layer and a vanilla custard top. It is a Dresden coffee-table classic.
how_to_eat: Eat a slice with afternoon coffee.
how_to_order: Buy at Saxon bakeries.

name: Leipziger Allerlei
description: A mix of young vegetables such as peas, carrots, green beans, asparagus heads, morels and celery, often with cauliflower and kohlrabi. It is named after Leipzig.
how_to_eat: Eat as a main or side.
how_to_order: Look for it on menus in Leipzig in spring.
